scenario: Finance's Monday report slows checkout. The orders database is General Purpose and already sits in a failover group with a readable secondary in UK West.
stem: What is the quickest safe fix?
options: Scale the primary up to twice the vCores for Monday mornings
Build a lakehouse and move the report to it this week
Point the report at the failover group's read-only listener
Turn on read scale-out on the General Purpose database
explanation: The geo-secondary already exists and is readable, so repointing the report moves the load off the primary today at no new cost. Read scale-out is not available on General Purpose, and scaling up pays to keep reports and checkout fighting on the same server.

stem: Azure SQL Database uses read committed snapshot by default. Why can a large report still slow checkout on the same database?
options: It competes for CPU, memory and tempdb, and pushes the pages checkout needs out of memory
Snapshot isolation is turned off whenever a query runs longer than a minute
Every SELECT takes shared table locks that block checkout's inserts until the whole report finishes
Reports always run at a higher priority than application queries
explanation: With row versioning, readers rarely block writers, so locks are not the main problem. The report consumes the same CPU, memory and tempdb that checkout needs. The locking answer is the tempting one, but it describes SQL Server's older default behaviour.

topic: when a replica is not enough
scenario: The report now runs on a readable replica and checkout is fine.
stem: Which new request most clearly needs an analytics platform rather than the replica?
options: Run the same report at 07:00 every Monday instead of 08:30, before the email goes out
Add a filter for orders over £100
Show the report to two more people in finance
Three years of margin by channel, joining ERP stock and the clickstream
explanation: A replica is a copy of one database with its current data only. History beyond what the shop keeps, and joins across several sources, need a separate analytical store. Running at a different time, adding a filter or adding viewers are all things the replica can already do.

stem: What does a lakehouse add to a plain data lake?
options: Faster object storage on premium SSDs
A table format with a transaction log, so lake files act as tables that SQL and Spark both read
A separate copy of every table loaded into a relational database, so that SQL users have something to query
Automatic deletion of raw files once they are cleaned
explanation: The transaction log over Parquet files is what turns a folder into a table with transactions, updates and a schema, while keeping one open copy. Copying data into a relational database is the old lake-plus-warehouse pattern the lakehouse avoids.

stem: In a medallion architecture, where do deduplicated orders with UTC times and one customer key across the shop and loyalty programme belong?
options: Bronze
Silver
Gold
The source database
explanation: Silver holds cleaned, conformed data. Bronze keeps data exactly as it landed, and gold holds business-ready star schemas and agreed measures built from silver. Conformed data is not yet a report-ready model, so it is not gold.

scenario: A transformation has calculated VAT wrongly for three months, and every gold revenue figure since July is off.
stem: What makes this fixable without asking the source systems for the data again?
options: The gold tables keep every previous version, so the figures from before July can be restored
Power BI caches the old figures
Bronze kept the raw data as it landed, so the corrected job can rebuild silver and gold
The read-only replica holds three months of history
explanation: Keeping raw data in bronze and transforming afterwards, ELT, means a fixed transformation can be rerun over history. Old versions of gold only contain the wrong numbers, and a replica holds today's state of the shop, not the data as it was.

stem: Why has ELT largely replaced ETL for new analytics platforms?
options: Cheap storage and elastic compute let you land raw data first and transform it in the platform
ELT tools come free with the platform, while ETL tools such as SSIS need separate licences
ELT does not need any scheduling
ETL cannot read from SQL Server
explanation: Landing raw first keeps the original data, so transformations can change and rerun, and the platform's own compute does the work. ELT jobs still run on schedules, usually as batch processing, so that option is wrong.

scenario: The CFO asks which reports use the net revenue column and where customers' email addresses are stored across all the data stores.
stem: Which service on the map answers that?
options: Azure Data Factory
Power BI
Azure Synapse Analytics
Microsoft Purview
explanation: Purview is the governance layer: it scans stores, classifies data such as email addresses and tracks lineage from sources to reports. Power BI shows the data but does not catalogue where personal data lives elsewhere, and Data Factory only moves data.
